notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2045.tlg001.perseus-: 348–349: Phaethon here is the Sun, whose course the Brahmans halt.
The finger-reckoning in 61–63 is obscure; the sense of 'the number that comes round again' is uncertain. 'Only-born' (μουνοτόκου) may mean an only child.
The subject of 'fanned up' (239) comes in the next line, outside the unit: the thousand snakes of Kampe's feet. Enyo, goddess of war, stands for battle.

nodes.text: seeking consoling oracles; for divinations
steal away griefs with hopes of what is to come.
Nor did old Astraios refuse; and of the only-born
girl, having grasped the measures of her nativity at the moment of birth,
and the time that does not stumble, and the course of the unerring Hour
of origin, he bent the fingers of his hands in turn
around the shifting cycle of the number that comes round again,
and measured it out from palm to palm with a twofold beat;
and at his command a servant, lifting the well-rounded
revolving sphere, the pattern of the heavens, the image of the cosmos,
Asterion, took it and set it beside him on the lid of a chest.
There the old man laboured, and, turning the tip of the axis,
he stretched his gaze around the zodiac circle,
looking this way and that, at both the fixed stars and the wanderers;
and he whirled the pole round; and with many-turning impulse
spying out the ever-changing shape of Lyaeus;
and she was angry with the guardians of Bromios; and, having received
from Achlys the treacherous flowers of a Thessalian herb,
she poured sleep over the head of the spellbound guards,
dripping sorcerous charms down over their hair;
and, smearing a delicate magic ointment over their faces,
she changed the former look of their human appearance;
on them appeared an eared shape of body,
and a horse's tail rose upright through their loins,
Whipping flesh-eating lions on against the Indian throng,
do not fear elephants, since your high-ruling Zeus
crushed high-headed Kampe with the thunderbolt,
whose whole body was twisted and many-formed; for a strange,
slanting, self-coiling Enyo [battle] they fanned up
I shoot the bear with arrows, and I cut the tree with the sword;
and I will gash the flank of the counterfeit lion.
But against you I arm the wise Brahmans, who bear no weapons;
for they are naked, and with god-summoning incantations
often the air-roaming one, like an unyoked bull,
they have drawn down from heaven and bewitched, the Moon;
and often, as he drove on his hastening chariot,
they have halted the course of restless Phaethon.
So he spoke, staring at the shape-changing apparitions of Bacchus;
and he kept an unbelieving mind; and with a purpose no charm could sway
